adarand.cite: Adarand Constructors, Inc. v. Peña, 515 U.S. 200 (1995)
adarand.held: Federal racial classifications are subject to strict scrutiny.

adkins.cite: Sunshine Anthracite Coal Co. v. Adkins, 310 U.S. 381 (1940)
adkins.held: Private bodies may assist government if they function subordinately to an agency that has final authority.

afpf.cite: Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, 594 U.S. 595 (2021)
afpf.held: Compelled disclosure of donor identities must be narrowly tailored to a sufficiently important interest (exacting scrutiny).

aiken.cite: In re Aiken County, 725 F.3d 255 (D.C. Cir. 2013)
aiken.held: An agency may not decline to follow a statutory mandate simply because it disagrees with it or lacks enthusiasm for it.

alabama_realtors.cite: Alabama Ass'n of Realtors v. HHS, 594 U.S. 758 (2021) (per curiam)
alabama_realtors.held: The CDC's nationwide eviction moratorium exceeded its authority under section 361 of the Public Health Service Act.

algonquin.cite: Federal Energy Administration v. Algonquin SNG, Inc., 426 U.S. 548 (1976)
algonquin.held: Section 232 lets the President adjust imports through license fees as well as quotas.

alpine.cite: Alpine Securities Corp. v. FINRA, 121 F.4th 1314 (D.C. Cir. 2024)
alpine.held: FINRA may not expel a member before the SEC has reviewed the expulsion (granting an injunction pending appeal).

amtrak.cite: Department of Transportation v. Association of American Railroads, 575 U.S. 43 (2015)
amtrak.held: Amtrak is a governmental entity for these purposes; the Court left the private-delegation questions for remand.

arthrex.cite: United States v. Arthrex, Inc., 594 U.S. 1 (2021)
arthrex.held: Administrative judges may not issue final decisions that no principal officer can review.

atlas_roofing.cite: Atlas Roofing Co. v. OSHRC, 430 U.S. 442 (1977)
atlas_roofing.held: Congress may assign new statutory 'public rights' (there, OSHA penalties) to agency adjudication without a jury; Jarkesy later confined this to claims without a common-law analogue.

austin.held: Civil forfeitures that serve in part to punish are subject to the Excessive Fines Clause.

axon.cite: Axon Enterprise, Inc. v. FTC, 598 U.S. 175 (2023)
axon.held: Parties may bring structural constitutional challenges to agency proceedings in federal district court without waiting for the agency to finish.

bajakajian.held: A punitive forfeiture violates the Excessive Fines Clause if grossly disproportional to the offense.

bi_metallic.cite: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization, 239 U.S. 441 (1915)
bi_metallic.held: Due process does not require a hearing before the government adopts a rule of general application; it protects particular parties singled out for action.

biden_missouri.held: Allowed the CMS rule requiring vaccination of staff at Medicare- and Medicaid-funded facilities to take effect.

boerne.cite: City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)
boerne.held: RFRA cannot be applied to the states, but it continues to bind the federal government.

burger.held: Warrantless inspections of closely regulated industries can be reasonable under set conditions.

carpenter.held: Acquiring historical cell-site location records is a search requiring a warrant.

carson.held: Government may not exclude religious organizations or uses from a generally available public benefit because they are religious.

carter_coal.cite: Carter v. Carter Coal Co., 298 U.S. 238 (1936)
carter_coal.held: Congress may not give private parties power to impose binding rules on their competitors.

catholic_charities.cite: Catholic Charities Bureau, Inc. v. Wisconsin Labor & Industry Review Comm'n, 605 U.S. ___ (2025)
catholic_charities.held: Government may not grant or deny a religious exemption based on theological distinctions between denominations.

cedar_point.cite: Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid, 594 U.S. 139 (2021)
cedar_point.held: A regulation granting a right to physically enter private property is a per se taking.

central_hudson.cite: Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Comm'n, 447 U.S. 557 (1980)
central_hudson.held: Sets the intermediate-scrutiny test for restrictions on commercial speech.

cfsa.cite: CFPB v. Community Financial Services Ass'n of America, 601 U.S. 416 (2024)
cfsa.held: The CFPB's funding mechanism satisfies the Appropriations Clause.

ch_dol_fiduciary.cite: Chamber of Commerce v. U.S. Department of Labor, 885 F.3d 360 (5th Cir. 2018)
ch_dol_fiduciary.held: Vacated the Department of Labor's 2016 fiduciary rule in its entirety as exceeding ERISA.

chamber_nlrb.cite: Chamber of Commerce v. NLRB, No. 6:23-cv-553 (E.D. Tex. Mar. 8, 2024)
chamber_nlrb.held: Vacated the NLRB's 2023 joint-employer rule as contrary to common-law agency principles the Act incorporates.

clinton_ny.cite: Clinton v. City of New York, 524 U.S. 417 (1998)
clinton_ny.held: The President may not cancel or amend parts of duly enacted statutes; the Line Item Veto Act is unconstitutional.

collins.held: An unconstitutional removal restriction does not by itself void the agency's actions; a challenger must show the restriction caused harm.

consumers_research.held: The Universal Service Fund survives nondelegation challenge, and the FCC's reliance on a private administrator is lawful because the administrator is subordinate to the FCC.

cook.held: On narrow, interim grounds, the Court (5 to 4) left in place a lower-court order keeping a Federal Reserve governor in office while her challenge to her removal proceeds, treating the Federal Reserve differently from other agencies.

creative_303.held: Government may not compel a person to create expressive work conveying a message she does not hold.

culley.held: Due process requires a timely forfeiture hearing but not a separate preliminary retention hearing.

cutter.held: RLUIPA's protections for institutionalized persons are a permissible accommodation of religion.

dames_moore.held: Upheld presidential actions under IEEPA settling claims against Iran, in light of congressional acquiescence.

dole.held: Congress may attach clear, related, non-coercive conditions to federal grants.

fcc_att.cite: FCC v. AT&T, Inc., No. 25-406 (U.S. June 4, 2026) (8 to 1)
fcc_att.held: FCC forfeiture orders do not violate the Seventh Amendment because they do not definitively resolve liability and the FCC's findings are not conclusive in a later collection suit.

fox.cite: FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 567 U.S. 239 (2012)
fox.held: Due process requires fair notice of what conduct is prohibited before an agency sanctions it.

franciscan.cite: Franciscan Alliance, Inc. v. Burwell, 227 F. Supp. 3d 660 (N.D. Tex. 2016)
franciscan.held: Enjoined parts of HHS's 2016 Section 1557 rule, finding them likely contrary to the statute and to RFRA as applied to religious health-care providers.

free_enterprise.cite: Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)
free_enterprise.held: Two layers of for-cause protection between the President and officers of the PCAOB violate the separation of powers.

fulton.cite: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, 593 U.S. 522 (2021)
fulton.held: A rule is not generally applicable if it allows individualized, discretionary exemptions; refusing one to a religious objector triggers strict scrutiny.

georgia_wheeler.cite: Georgia v. Wheeler, 418 F. Supp. 3d 1336 (S.D. Ga. 2019)
georgia_wheeler.held: Held the 2015 Clean Water Rule unlawful as exceeding the agencies' authority under the Clean Water Act.

granfinanciera.held: Congress may not strip a jury right from a claim resembling a common-law action by assigning it to a non-Article III forum.

hobby_lobby.cite: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., 573 U.S. 682 (2014)
hobby_lobby.held: The HHS contraceptive mandate, as applied to closely held corporations with religious objections, violated RFRA because less restrictive means were available.

holt.held: Under RLUIPA a prison grooming rule that barred a religious beard was not the least restrictive means.

ica.held: Statute: the President may propose deferrals and rescissions but may not withhold appropriated funds without following the Act.

jarkesy.held: When the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitles the defendant to a jury, and the public-rights exception does not apply.

jaycees.cite: Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609 (1984)
jaycees.held: Freedom of expressive association may be infringed only by regulations serving compelling interests unrelated to suppressing ideas that cannot be achieved by less restrictive means.

kennedy.cite: Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)
kennedy.held: Establishment Clause questions are decided by historical practice and understanding, not the Lemon test; government may not punish private religious expression.

kisor.held: Deference to an agency's reading of its own regulation survives only for genuinely ambiguous rules and within strict limits.

larson.held: Laws that grant denominational preferences are subject to strict scrutiny under the Establishment Clause.

learning_resources.cite: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (U.S. Feb. 20, 2026)
learning_resources.held: The International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.

little_sisters.cite: Little Sisters of the Poor v. Pennsylvania, 591 U.S. 657 (2020)
little_sisters.held: Agencies may, and in some cases must, consider RFRA when writing rules, and may create religious exemptions.

loper_bright.cite: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)
loper_bright.held: Courts must exercise independent judgment on statutory meaning and may not defer to an agency's reading because a statute is ambiguous; Chevron is overruled.

lucia.held: SEC administrative law judges are officers of the United States and must be appointed as the Appointments Clause requires.

lukumi.cite: Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993)
lukumi.held: A law that targets religious practice or is not neutral and generally applicable must satisfy strict scrutiny.

mahmoud.held: Government policies that substantially interfere with parents' religious upbringing of their children trigger strict scrutiny, even if neutral and generally applicable.

mathews.held: The process due before a deprivation is set by balancing the private interest, the risk of error, and the government's interest.

moody.held: A platform's curation of third-party content is protected expression; government may not override it to rebalance the marketplace of ideas.

murphy.held: Congress may not directly order state legislatures what laws to pass or not pass.

murthy.held: Plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge federal officials' communications with platforms about content moderation.

myers.held: The President has power to remove executive officers he appoints.

naacp_alabama.cite: NAACP v. Alabama ex rel. Patterson, 357 U.S. 449 (1958)
naacp_alabama.held: Compelled disclosure of an association's membership lists can unconstitutionally burden freedom of association.

napfm.cite: National Ass'n of Private Fund Managers v. SEC, 103 F.4th 1097 (5th Cir. 2024)
napfm.held: Vacated the SEC's private fund adviser rules as exceeding its statutory authority.

nebraska.held: The student-loan forgiveness program exceeded the HEROES Act; the major questions doctrine reinforced that reading.

nebraska_press.cite: Nebraska Press Ass'n v. Stuart, 427 U.S. 539 (1976)
nebraska_press.held: Prior restraints on speech bear a heavy presumption against their validity.

nevada_dol.cite: Nevada v. U.S. Department of Labor, 275 F. Supp. 3d 795 (E.D. Tex. 2017)
nevada_dol.held: Held the Department of Labor's 2016 overtime rule invalid as exceeding the Fair Labor Standards Act.

nfib_osha.held: OSHA's workplace vaccine-or-test mandate likely exceeded its statutory authority; the Court stayed it.

nfib_sebelius.held: Conditions on federal funds become unconstitutionally coercive when they threaten existing funding the states depend on.

nifla.cite: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra, 585 U.S. 755 (2018)
nifla.held: Compelled notices that are not purely factual and uncontroversial information about the speaker's own services fall outside Zauderer and face heightened scrutiny.

o_centro.cite: Gonzales v. O Centro Espírita Beneficente União do Vegetal, 546 U.S. 418 (2006)
o_centro.held: Under RFRA the government must justify applying a law to the particular religious claimant, not just the law in general.

ohio_telecom.cite: Ohio Telecom Ass'n v. FCC, 124 F.4th 993 (6th Cir. 2025)
ohio_telecom.held: Set aside the FCC's 2024 net-neutrality order; broadband is an information service the FCC may not regulate as common carriage.

patel.cite: City of Los Angeles v. Patel, 576 U.S. 409 (2015)
patel.held: A demand for business records without an opportunity for precompliance review by a neutral decisionmaker is unconstitutional.

powell.held: Upheld the SEC's no-deny settlement policy against a facial First Amendment challenge, while recognizing legitimate concerns; the SEC rescinded the policy in May 2026.

printz.held: The federal government may not command state officers to administer federal programs.

reed.cite: Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155 (2015)
reed.held: Laws that regulate speech because of its topic or message are content-based and must satisfy strict scrutiny.

rfra_statute.cite: Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, 42 U.S.C. 2000bb to 2000bb-4
rfra_statute.held: Statute: the federal government may not substantially burden a person's religious exercise, even by a neutral and generally applicable rule, unless it uses the least restrictive means of furthering a compelling interest.

rluipa_statute.cite: Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000, 42 U.S.C. 2000cc to 2000cc-5
rluipa_statute.held: Statute: applies RFRA's strict-scrutiny test to land-use regulation and to prisons and other institutions that receive federal funds.

romeril.held: Declined to relieve a defendant from a consent judgment's no-deny provision.

rumery.cite: Town of Newton v. Rumery, 480 U.S. 386 (1987)
rumery.held: Agreements waiving constitutional rights can be enforced if voluntary and not against public policy.

ryan_ftc.cite: Ryan, LLC v. FTC, 746 F. Supp. 3d 369 (N.D. Tex. 2024)
ryan_ftc.held: Set aside the FTC's non-compete rule as exceeding the FTC's rulemaking authority and as arbitrary and capricious.

sackett.held: The Clean Water Act reaches only wetlands with a continuous surface connection to traditional waters; the 'significant nexus' test is rejected.

see_seattle.cite: See v. City of Seattle, 387 U.S. 541 (1967)
see_seattle.held: Administrative inspections of commercial premises generally require a warrant.

seila.cite: Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020)
seila.held: For-cause removal protection for the CFPB's single director is unconstitutional.

sffa.cite: Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, 600 U.S. 181 (2023)
sffa.held: Race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and UNC violate equal protection.

slaughter.held: Statutory limits on the President's power to remove FTC commissioners are unconstitutional; Humphrey's Executor is overruled.

smith.held: A neutral, generally applicable law that incidentally burdens religious exercise does not violate the Free Exercise Clause.

sorrell.cite: Sorrell v. IMS Health Inc., 564 U.S. 552 (2011)
sorrell.held: Content- and speaker-based burdens on commercial information receive heightened scrutiny.

tandon.held: A rule triggers strict scrutiny when it treats any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise.

tanzin.held: RFRA permits damages suits against federal officials in their individual capacities.

texas_dol_2024.cite: Texas v. U.S. Department of Labor, No. 4:24-cv-499 (E.D. Tex. Nov. 15, 2024)
texas_dol_2024.held: Vacated the Department of Labor's 2024 overtime rule as exceeding the Fair Labor Standards Act.

timbs.held: The Excessive Fines Clause applies to the states.

train.cite: Train v. City of New York, 420 U.S. 35 (1975)
train.held: The executive may not withhold funds Congress directed be allotted.

trump_hawaii.held: Upheld a presidential proclamation restricting entry under INA section 212(f).

tull.held: Civil penalties are a legal remedy, so the defendant is entitled to a jury on liability in a government penalty suit.

vmi.held: Sex-based government classifications require an exceedingly persuasive justification.

vullo.held: A regulator may not coerce third parties to punish or suppress protected speech.

west_virginia.held: Agencies need clear congressional authorization to decide questions of vast economic and political significance; the Clean Power Plan's generation-shifting approach exceeded the Clean Air Act.

youngstown.cite: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 (1952)
youngstown.held: The President may not make law without constitutional or statutory authority; Justice Jackson's three-category framework.

zauderer.cite: Zauderer v. Office of Disciplinary Counsel, 471 U.S. 626 (1985)
zauderer.held: Compelled factual, uncontroversial commercial disclosures are permissible if reasonably related to preventing deception and not unduly burdensome.

elements.text: A civil penalty or similar punitive money remedy is sought
The claim resembles a common-law action (fraud, misrepresentation, deception)
The matter is decided in the agency's own forum

issues.label: Agency adjudication of penalties (jury trial and Article III)
open_questions: How far Jarkesy reaches beyond fraud-like claims (for example, purely regulatory violations).
Whether consent settlements negotiated under threat of in-house proceedings raise separate concerns.
How FCC v. AT&T's reasoning applies to other agencies whose penalty orders are not self-executing.

precedent.label: Direct holding
precedent.note: An SEC penalty claim for fraud decided in-house: the facts of Jarkesy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A fraud-like penalty claim at another agency: Jarkesy applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: No common-law analogue found: whether Jarkesy reaches purely statutory penalty claims (Atlas Roofing) is open.

issues.question: Is an agency deciding, in its own forum and without a jury, a penalty claim of the kind the Seventh Amendment and Article III reserve to the courts?
issues.test: Under Jarkesy the Seventh Amendment jury right attaches when (1) the government seeks a legal remedy such as a civil penalty (2) for a claim that resembles a common-law action, fraud being the paradigm. When such a claim is (3) decided in the agency's own forum, the defendant is denied a jury. The public-rights exception (customs, immigration, public lands, benefits, taxes) is weighed against a violation. FCC v. AT&T (2026) upheld FCC forfeiture orders because they do not definitively resolve liability.

weighed.text: Described as settled or consented. Noted only: a settlement does not cure the forum, and people settle for many reasons.
FCC forfeiture order or notice of apparent liability: the Supreme Court upheld this practice in FCC v. AT&T (2026)
Subject matter traditionally treated as a public right (customs, immigration, public lands, benefits, taxes)

elements.text: An adjudicator or officer (ALJ, hearing officer, administrative judge, board member) is involved
The official decides cases or issues binding decisions
The document describes an appointment, review, or removal defect

issues.label: Appointment and review of officers (ALJs, hearing officers, and board members)
open_questions: Whether multi-level removal protection for ALJs survives after Free Enterprise Fund and Slaughter.
What remedy follows a removal defect after Collins v. Yellen.

precedent.label: Direct holding
precedent.note: Lucia and Arthrex hold that unappointed or unreviewable adjudicators violate Article II.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: No specific appointment or review defect is described.

issues.question: Are officials exercising significant federal authority appointed and reviewable as Article II requires?
issues.test: An official who holds a continuing position and exercises significant authority under federal law is an officer (Lucia) and must be appointed by the President, a department head, or a court of law; an inferior officer's final decisions must be reviewable by a principal officer (Arthrex). Ratification by a properly appointed official cures an appointment defect going forward, so ratification notices are not flagged.

elements.text: Issued by a private, agency-supervised corporation
The action binds members or the public (a rule or fee change)
Effective without prior agency approval (for example, immediately effective under 19(b)(3)(A))

issues.label: Government power exercised by a private corporation
open_questions: Whether immediately effective rule and fee changes give the SEC enough prior control.
Whether FINRA and the exchanges are themselves government actors for constitutional purposes.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Open question: Consumers' Research upheld a subordinate private administrator; Alpine addressed discipline, not rules.

issues.question: Is a private self-regulatory organization exercising government power without adequate agency control?
issues.test: Private bodies may help administer federal law only if they function subordinately to an agency that retains final authority (Adkins; Consumers' Research). Delegating binding power to private parties without that control is forbidden (Carter Coal). Because no court has applied this to the thousands of routine immediately effective filings, they are listed as possible issues rather than rated.

elements.text: A private, agency-supervised corporation
Discipline is imposed or proposed
The sanction is expulsion or a bar

issues.label: Private corporation disciplining or expelling a member
open_questions: Whether Alpine's reasoning extends to fines and suspensions, and outside the D.C. Circuit.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Expulsion or a bar: a federal court of appeals has held this practice unlawful (Alpine).

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Alpine addressed expulsion; lesser discipline is an open question.

issues.question: Is a private self-regulatory organization imposing severe discipline before any government review?
issues.test: The D.C. Circuit has held that FINRA may not expel a member before the SEC reviews the expulsion (Alpine).

elements.text: A binding rule, order, or program
Vast economic or political significance (designated economically significant or major, or billions of dollars or a whole industry at stake)
A novel or expansive claim of power (unprecedented, first-ever, newly asserted authority, emergency standard, moratorium)
Rests on a broad or general grant of power (a general rulemaking or catch-all provision, or an emergency statute)

issues.label: Agency authority, delegation, and major questions
open_questions: What counts as 'vast' significance, and whether the doctrine applies to deregulatory rules.
Whether the major questions doctrine applies to the President's own actions as it does to agencies.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Significance, a novel claim of power, and a thin statutory basis together: West Virginia v. EPA, Alabama Realtors, and NFIB v. OSHA apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Significance alone, or without a novel claim of power, is an open question.

issues.question: Does the action decide a question of vast economic or political significance, or claim a power, without clear congressional authorization?
issues.test: The executive branch has only the powers the Constitution and Congress give it. Agencies need clear congressional authorization for rules of vast economic and political significance, especially when they claim newfound power in a long-standing statute (West Virginia v. EPA; Alabama Realtors; NFIB v. OSHA; Biden v. Nebraska).

elements.text: The agency interprets a statute
The agency invokes ambiguity, silence, or gap-filling
The agency relies on deference to its own reading (Chevron)

issues.label: Agency interpretation of an ambiguous statute (Chevron and Loper Bright)
open_questions: How much weight courts still give agency views under Skidmore after Loper Bright.
Which rules upheld under Chevron can be challenged again after Loper Bright and Corner Post.

precedent.label: Direct holding
precedent.note: Loper Bright overruled Chevron, so reliance on Chevron deference is open to challenge; rated Likely at most because Loper Bright preserved earlier cases upholding rules under Chevron.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Interpretation without claimed deference is ordinary agency work.

issues.question: Does the action rest on deference to the agency's own reading of a statute?
issues.test: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron: courts, not agencies, decide what statutes mean, and they may not defer to an agency's reading because a statute is ambiguous. An action that rests on Chevron deference is therefore open to challenge. Loper Bright also said earlier cases that upheld rules under Chevron keep their force, so these flags are rated Likely (arguable) rather than higher.

weighed.text: Issued after Loper Bright and discusses it, which usually means the agency is explaining that it does not rely on Chevron

elements.text: The action removes, or directs the decisions of, agency leaders
The body is one the Court still treats as protected (the Federal Reserve)

issues.label: Presidential control and removal of agency leaders
open_questions: Which bodies, beyond the Federal Reserve, remain outside the President's at-will removal power.
What process is due before removing a Federal Reserve governor for cause (Cook remains in litigation).

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Federal Reserve governors: Trump v. Cook applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: After Slaughter, presidential removal of other commissioners is generally lawful.

issues.question: Does the action remove or direct officials whose independence the law still protects?
issues.test: After Trump v. Slaughter (2026), the President may remove commissioners of agencies wielding executive power. The Federal Reserve is treated differently: in Trump v. Cook (2026) the Court, on narrow interim grounds, left in place a lower-court order keeping a Federal Reserve governor in office.

elements.text: Appropriated money is withheld, paused, frozen, or terminated
The action is broad (a whole program, a category of awards, or government-wide)
The reason given is policy disagreement rather than a statutory ground

issues.label: Spending, funding, and appropriations
open_questions: Whether courts will enforce the Impoundment Control Act at the behest of private grantees.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Broad or policy-based withholding of appropriated funds: Train and the Impoundment Control Act apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: A narrow funding action is an open question.

issues.question: Is the executive withholding or redirecting money contrary to Congress's appropriations?
issues.test: Congress holds the power of the purse. The executive must spend funds as Congress directs (Train) and may withhold them only through the Impoundment Control Act's procedures. Withholding broad categories of funds for policy reasons, rather than for reasons the statute allows, is the core concern.

weighed.text: The President sent a special message under the Impoundment Control Act

elements.text: Abolishes, eliminates, or dismantles an office or agency
Done by executive action rather than statute
The body or function was created by statute

issues.label: Creating, abolishing, or restructuring agencies and offices
open_questions: Whether large reductions in force can effectively abolish a statutory function.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A statutory body or function is abandoned: Aiken County and Youngstown apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Courts are still working out the limits of executive reorganization.

issues.question: Is the executive restructuring or abolishing a body that Congress created by statute?
issues.test: Congress creates agencies and assigns their functions by statute; the executive may manage but not abolish them or abandon their statutory duties without authority (Youngstown framework; In re Aiken County).

elements.text: The action is directed at state or local governments
It commands state officials or legislatures
It conditions existing federal funds on compliance

issues.label: Federalism (commandeering and conditions on federal funds)
open_questions: When executive (rather than congressional) funding conditions are unauthorized as well as coercive.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A command to state officials: Printz and Murphy apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Existing funds conditioned on compliance: NFIB v. Sebelius applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Ordinary grant conditions are usually lawful.

issues.question: Does the action command state officials or coerce states through funding conditions?
issues.test: The federal government may not commandeer state officers or legislatures (Printz; Murphy) and may not attach coercive conditions to existing funds (NFIB v. Sebelius); conditions must be clear and related (Dole).

elements.text: Imposes duties, tariffs, or prohibitions on the public, or suspends or refuses to enforce a statute
Rests on an emergency power or a general statute rather than a specific grant
The power claimed is one the cited statute does not give (tariffs under IEEPA), or the action suspends a statute without congressional authorization
Applies to private parties (importers, businesses, people), not just to agencies

issues.label: Executive action that makes law (emergency powers, tariffs, and suspending statutes)
open_questions: The limits of tariff authority under Sections 122, 232, and 301 after Learning Resources.
Whether the major questions doctrine constrains the President directly, or only agencies.
When nonenforcement policies become a refusal to execute the law.

precedent.label: Direct holding
precedent.note: Tariffs or duties imposed under IEEPA: the facts of Learning Resources.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Suspending or refusing to enforce a statute without congressional authorization: Clinton v. City of New York and In re Aiken County apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Other IEEPA measures that operate like taxes or regulation of commerce: Learning Resources applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Other bases (Sections 232, 301, 122, 212(f), and emergency statutes) are open questions under Youngstown.

issues.question: Does an executive action impose duties, taxes, or prohibitions on the public, or set aside a statute, without a power the Constitution or Congress actually gives?
issues.test: The President's power to act must come from the Constitution or a statute (Youngstown). Taxes and tariffs are Congress's power (Art. I, sec. 8), and IEEPA does not delegate it (Learning Resources). The executive may not cancel or suspend duly enacted statutes (Clinton v. City of New York; In re Aiken County). Waivers and exemptions that Congress itself authorized are not flagged. Other trade and entry statutes (Sections 232, 301, 122, and 212(f)) are checked one by one.

weighed.text: Also rests on a trade statute courts have read broadly (Section 232, 301, 122, or 201)
Restricts entry of noncitizens under INA 212(f), which Trump v. Hawaii read broadly

elements.text: A restriction on speaking about the matter
Imposed by a government order or settlement
Applies to public statements

issues.label: Gag orders, no-deny terms, and prior restraints on speech
open_questions: Whether the Supreme Court will review no-deny provisions, and whether rescission moots the issue.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Prior-restraint doctrine applies, but courts have upheld these terms so far; the question remains contested.

issues.question: Does the government condition a settlement or order on silence about the case?
issues.test: Prior restraints are presumptively invalid (Nebraska Press). Courts of appeals have so far upheld no-deny settlement terms as voluntary waivers (Powell; Romeril; Rumery), so the issue is arguable but contested.

weighed.text: Courts of appeals have upheld no-deny terms as voluntary waivers (Powell; Romeril)

elements.text: Regulates or compels speech, advertising, warnings, publishing, broadcasting, or editorial choices
Content-based, viewpoint-based, or compelled
Compels opinion or controversial statements, or targets protected expression or editorial judgment

issues.label: Freedom of speech and the press
open_questions: How Zauderer applies to disclosures that are arguably not purely factual or uncontroversial (for example, climate or ESG disclosures).
How Moody applies to agency rules affecting platform moderation.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Pressure on third parties to suppress speech: Vullo applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Content-based restrictions or compelled non-factual statements: NIFLA and Reed apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Outcome depends on the level of scrutiny and the fit of the rule.

issues.question: Does the action restrict or compel speech, or pressure others to suppress it?
issues.test: Content-based restrictions face strict scrutiny (Reed); commercial-speech restrictions face intermediate scrutiny (Central Hudson), heightened when speaker- or content-based (Sorrell). Compelled disclosures are allowed when purely factual, uncontroversial, and reasonably related to preventing deception (Zauderer); compelled opinions or controversial statements face heightened scrutiny (NIFLA). Government may not compel expressive work (303 Creative), override editorial judgment (Moody), or coerce third parties to suppress speech (Vullo).

weighed.text: Requires only purely factual, uncontroversial information about the speaker's own products or services (Zauderer)

elements.text: Affects religious exercise, religious organizations, or houses of worship
Imposes a requirement, penalty, exclusion, or loss of benefits that bears on that exercise
Not neutral or generally applicable (singles out religion, has secular exemptions, or discretionary exemptions)
No religious exemption or accommodation is provided, or one is removed

issues.label: Religious liberty (Free Exercise, Establishment Clause, RFRA, and RLUIPA)
open_questions: Whether the Court will overrule Smith (several Justices have urged it).
How Mahmoud's parental-rights reasoning applies to federal programs and conditions on funds.
How RLUIPA applies when federal agencies set conditions for state prisons or land-use programs.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Lines drawn between denominations or a religious test: Larson and Catholic Charities apply by close analogy (Establishment Clause).

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Prisons, detention, or land use: RLUIPA (and, for federal action, RFRA) applies by close analogy (Holt).

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Not neutral or generally applicable, with no accommodation: Fulton, Tandon, and Lukumi apply by close analogy; for federal action RFRA independently requires strict scrutiny.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A federal requirement that burdens religious exercise without accommodation: RFRA and Hobby Lobby apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Religious groups excluded from a public benefit: Carson v. Makin applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: A neutral, generally applicable rule gets rational-basis review under Smith, but RFRA still requires strict scrutiny of substantial burdens imposed by the federal government.

issues.question: Does the action burden religious exercise, discriminate against religion, or favor one religion over another?
issues.test: Free Exercise: a neutral, generally applicable rule that incidentally burdens religion gets rational-basis review (Smith); a rule that targets religion, allows individualized exemptions (Fulton), or treats comparable secular activity better (Tandon) must survive strict scrutiny (Lukumi). Government may not exclude religious groups from public benefits because they are religious (Carson). Establishment Clause: government may not prefer one denomination over another (Larson; Catholic Charities). RFRA: for federal action, a substantial burden on religious exercise must be the least restrictive means of serving a compelling interest, even under a neutral rule (Hobby Lobby). RLUIPA applies the same test to land-use rules and to prisons and other institutions that receive federal funds (Holt).

weighed.text: Provides a religious exemption or accommodation

elements.text: Requires disclosure of members, donors, owners, or supporters, or penalizes association
Applies in bulk rather than case by case
The information may be made public or shared widely

issues.label: Freedom of association and donor privacy
open_questions: How Americans for Prosperity applies to federal beneficial-ownership and political-disclosure rules.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: Bulk donor or member disclosure that may become public: Americans for Prosperity applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Disclosure rules are judged by exacting scrutiny case by case.

issues.question: Does the action compel disclosure of members or donors, or penalize joining or supporting a group?
issues.test: Compelled disclosure of members or donors must survive exacting scrutiny: narrow tailoring to a sufficiently important interest (Americans for Prosperity; NAACP v. Alabama). Burdens on expressive association need a compelling interest unrelated to suppressing ideas (Roberts v. Jaycees).

elements.text: A search, inspection, or demand for records or data
Without a warrant or precompliance review

issues.label: Searches, inspections, records demands, or surveillance
open_questions: How Carpenter applies to bulk data demands made to companies about their customers.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A search or records demand without a warrant or precompliance review: See v. Seattle and Patel apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Ordinary inspections and subpoenas are usually lawful.

issues.question: Does the action authorize searches or records demands without a warrant or neutral review?
issues.test: Administrative inspections generally require a warrant (See v. Seattle), and records demands require a chance for precompliance review (Patel), except in closely regulated industries (Burger). Historical location records require a warrant (Carpenter).

weighed.text: A closely regulated industry (the Burger exception may apply)

elements.text: Property, money, or a license is taken, seized, revoked, or suspended
Directed at particular parties (an enforcement or adjudicative action), or a rule granting physical access
Without prior notice, a hearing, or fair notice of the standard; or a right of physical access to property
A physical occupation or right of access to private property

issues.label: Property, takings, or due process
open_questions: When summary suspensions of licenses are justified by emergencies without a prior hearing.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A right of physical access to private property: Cedar Point applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A deprivation imposed on particular parties without notice or a hearing: Mathews and Fox apply by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Due process is a fact-specific balance.

issues.question: Does an action against particular parties take property or a license without the notice and hearing due process requires, or does a rule take property by granting physical access?
issues.test: Due process applies to actions directed at particular parties, not to rules of general application (Bi-Metallic). The process due turns on the Mathews balance, and agencies must give fair notice of prohibited conduct before sanctioning it (Fox). A rule granting a right of physical access to private property is a per se taking (Cedar Point).

elements.text: A punitive fine, penalty, or forfeiture
The amount is at least $1 million
The underlying violation is described as technical, recordkeeping, or reporting only

issues.label: Excessive fines and forfeitures
open_questions: How courts measure proportionality for corporate penalties calculated per violation.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: A large punitive sum for a technical violation: Bajakajian applies by close analogy.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Gross disproportionality is fact-specific; amounts alone are a screen.

issues.question: Is a punitive penalty or forfeiture grossly disproportional to the offense?
issues.test: Punitive fines and forfeitures violate the Eighth Amendment if grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense (Bajakajian); civil forfeitures that partly punish are covered (Austin).

weighed.text: The money is described as restitution to victims, which is generally remedial

elements.text: The action classifies by race or sex
It grants an express preference, presumption, set-aside, or quota based on race or sex

issues.label: Classifications by race, sex, or other protected traits
open_questions: How SFFA applies to federal contracting presumptions of disadvantage.

precedent.label: Close analogy
precedent.note: An express racial or sex preference: SFFA and Adarand apply by close analogy; strict scrutiny is rarely satisfied.

precedent.label: Open question
precedent.note: Mentions of diversity programs are not themselves classifications.

issues.question: Does the action classify people by race or sex?
issues.test: Federal racial classifications receive strict scrutiny (Adarand) and are rarely upheld after SFFA; sex classifications require an exceedingly persuasive justification (Virginia).

constitutionality: The rating measures one thing: how likely it is that the action is unlawful under the Constitution or the limits on executive power, under the law as it stands today. Impact is recorded separately and never affects it.
Each memo states a test broken into elements. Gate elements are the essential ones: an issue is rated only when every gate element appears; otherwise it is listed as a possible issue.

Precedent strength comes from the first rule in the memo that matches: a direct holding (a court has held this practice unlawful), a close analogy (a Supreme Court holding applies closely, or an appeals court has held the same practice unlawful), or an open question.

Likely unlawful is generous, because RegCollect is built to surface arguable issues: the gate elements and at least half of all elements, with any precedent. Very likely unlawful: a direct holding with at least half the elements, or a close analogy with every element. Almost certainly unlawful: a direct holding with every element.

Very likely and almost certainly require the elements to appear in the document's operative text: its title, action line, and summary; the whole of a presidential document; or a rule's authority line and regulatory text. Elements found only in other passages of the full text (preambles, comment responses) can support Likely at most. Each flag says which elements came from the full text.

Weighed factors (such as a closely regulated industry) lower the rating by one step each but never below Likely. When the Supreme Court has upheld the very practice (for example, FCC forfeiture orders in FCC v. AT&T), the issue is listed as a possible issue with that reason. Settlements are noted only.

When a court has ruled on the specific action, the ruling sets the rating: Supreme Court, almost certainly; court of appeals, very likely; district court, likely. Each such flag states what the court held. A ruling that upheld the action lowers the rating one step.
Some memos cap their ratings: reliance on Chevron deference is rated Likely at most, because Loper Bright preserved earlier cases that upheld rules under Chevron.
Ratings apply today's law. When the controlling decision came after the action, the flag notes that the action may have been lawful under the precedent at the time.
impact: Impact is noted for context only. It is not color-coded and does not affect the lawfulness rating.

Sanction points: 4 for criminal charges, bars, expulsions, debarment, revocations, and practice bans; 3 for civil penalties, forfeitures, disgorgement, seizures, asset freezes, and funding cuts; 2 for cease-and-desist orders, injunctions, suspensions, denials, shutdowns, gag terms, trading halts, data-deletion orders, monitors, recalls, and import actions; 1 for warnings, censures, subpoenas, inspections, compelled notices, restitution, and settlements.
Money points: 3 for at least $100 million, 2 for at least $1 million, 1 for any stated amount.

Reach points: 3 for presidential documents and rules designated economically significant or major; 2 for other final or proposed rules; 1 for actions against particular parties and self-regulatory filings.
Lower Impact: 1 to 3 points. Significant Impact: 4 to 6. Serious Impact: 7 or more.

rulings.label: IEEPA tariff orders
rulings.summary: The Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, so the duties imposed by these orders lacked legal authority. Tariffs are a power the Constitution gives Congress.

rulings.label: Clean Power Plan
rulings.summary: The Supreme Court held that the Clean Power Plan's generation-shifting approach exceeded EPA's authority under section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act (major questions doctrine).

rulings.label: CDC eviction moratorium
rulings.summary: The Supreme Court held that the CDC's nationwide eviction moratorium exceeded its authority under the Public Health Service Act.

rulings.caution: The Supreme Court ruled on a stay application, not a final judgment; OSHA later withdrew the standard. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: OSHA vaccine-or-test emergency standard
rulings.summary: The Supreme Court stayed the standard, holding that challengers were likely to succeed because OSHA likely lacked authority. Because the ruling was a stay rather than a final judgment, it is rated very likely rather than almost certain.

rulings.label: CMS health-care staff vaccination rule
rulings.summary: The Supreme Court allowed this rule to take effect, finding it within the Secretary's authority.

rulings.caution: District court ruling; the 2015 rule was later repealed and replaced. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: 2015 Clean Water Rule
rulings.summary: A federal district court held the rule unlawful, and Sackett v. EPA (2023) later rejected the 'significant nexus' approach it relied on.

rulings.caution: One court of appeals (Fifth Circuit). Verify before relying.
rulings.label: Department of Labor fiduciary rule (2016)
rulings.summary: The Fifth Circuit vacated the rule in its entirety as exceeding ERISA.

rulings.caution: One court of appeals (Sixth Circuit). Verify before relying.
rulings.label: FCC net-neutrality order (2024)
rulings.summary: The Sixth Circuit, applying Loper Bright without deference, set the order aside as beyond the FCC's statutory authority.

rulings.caution: One court of appeals (Fifth Circuit). Verify before relying.
rulings.label: SEC private fund adviser rules
rulings.summary: The Fifth Circuit vacated the rules as exceeding the SEC's statutory authority.

rulings.caution: District court ruling; the FTC later dropped its appeals. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: FTC non-compete rule
rulings.summary: A federal district court set the rule aside nationwide as exceeding the FTC's rulemaking authority.

rulings.caution: District court ruling. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: Department of Labor overtime rule (2024)
rulings.summary: A federal district court vacated the rule as exceeding the Fair Labor Standards Act.

rulings.caution: District court ruling. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: Department of Labor overtime rule (2016)
rulings.summary: A federal district court held the rule invalid as exceeding the Fair Labor Standards Act.

rulings.caution: District court ruling. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: NLRB joint-employer rule (2023)
rulings.summary: A federal district court vacated the rule.

rulings.caution: District court ruling, later followed by further litigation and new rules. Verify before relying.
rulings.label: HHS Section 1557 rule (2016)
rulings.summary: A federal district court enjoined parts of the rule, finding them likely contrary to the statute and to RFRA as applied to religious health-care providers.
